title: Online Stock Span
description: Brute force to optimized: walking backward day by day versus a monotonic stack of (price, span) pairs that absorbs whole prior runs in amortized O(1).

blocks.text: Design an algorithm that collects daily price quotes for a stock and returns the SPAN of the stock's price for the current day. The span of a stock's price today is the maximum number of consecutive days (starting from today and going backward) for which the price was less than or equal to today's price. Implement the StockSpanner class: the constructor initializes the object, and next(price) returns the span of that day's stock price.

blocks.caption: A monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs computes each day's span in amortized O(1), absorbing every earlier day it dominates

blocks.text: Each day's span counts how far back (consecutively) the price stays less than or equal to today's price; crucially, if an earlier day ALREADY had a large span (because it, in turn, dominated several days before it), that entire span can be "absorbed" into today's span in one step, rather than re-counting day by day.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Growing Wave That Swallows Whatever It's Taller Than
blocks.text: Imagine tracking daily high-water marks, where today's span is "how many consecutive prior days' water levels were at or below today's." If yesterday's water level ALREADY swallowed several days before it (because it too was higher than a whole streak), and today is even higher than yesterday, today doesn't need to re-check each of those older days individually: it can simply "absorb" yesterday's entire streak length in one step, since anything yesterday dominated, today (being even higher) also dominates.

blocks.caption: Whenever a new price is >= the stack's top price, that top entry's ENTIRE span gets absorbed directly into the running total for today

blocks.text: Before recomputing each day's span by walking backward day-by-day through EVERY previous price (redundant, since earlier spans already summarize entire chunks of history), notice that a monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs lets each new day absorb WHOLE previously-computed spans at once.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If today's price is >= the price at the top of the stack, then EVERYTHING that top entry's span already covers is ALSO covered by today (since today is even higher), so that entire span can be absorbed in a single step, without individually re-checking each of those days.

Observation 2: Repeating this absorption (popping and adding spans) while the stack's top price keeps qualifying correctly accumulates the FULL consecutive run backward from today.

Observation 3: Once a price is found that is STRICTLY GREATER than today's (or the stack becomes empty), the run stops there, since that day breaks the "less than or equal" streak.

Observation 4: Pushing today's own (price, span) pair onto the stack makes it available for FUTURE days to potentially absorb in the exact same way.

Recognizing that a previously resolved span can be absorbed WHOLESALE (not re-walked day by day) is the key insight that makes this efficient even though prices stream in one at a time.
This is a monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs: each new day absorbs entire previously-computed spans in amortized O(1) time, rather than re-walking day by day.

Remember every price seen so far in a simple list; for each new price, walk backward through that list, counting consecutive days whose price is <= today's, until a strictly greater price (or the beginning) is reached.

items: Maintain a list of every price seen so far, in order.
For each new price, walk backward from the most recent entry, counting how many consecutive entries have price <= today's, stopping at the first one that is strictly greater (or the very beginning).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Remembering every price in order directly enables the backward walk required by the span's definition.
This directly mirrors the definition, but re-checks every individual day in the worst case, even ones that a previous day's span had already "resolved."

blocks.text: Correctly computes each day's span, since walking backward day by day directly matches the problem's definition.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per call in the worst case (a strictly increasing price sequence, where every new price extends all the way back to day 1), O(n^2) total across n calls.
Space: O(n), for the list of all prices seen so far.
Limitation: re-walking day by day ignores that earlier days' spans ALREADY summarize entire consecutive runs; absorbing those spans wholesale achieves the same result in amortized O(1) per call.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force re-walks individual days, even ones already "covered" by an earlier resolved span. Instead, maintain a monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs. For each new price, repeatedly pop and ADD the span of any stack-top entry whose price is <= today's price (absorbing that entire resolved run at once), until a strictly greater price remains (or the stack empties). Push today's own (price, accumulated span) pair for future days to potentially absorb.

Maintain a stack of (price, span) pairs. For next(price): initialize span = 1; while the stack is non-empty and its top price is <= price, pop it and add its span to the running total; push (price, span) onto the stack; return span.
Use a monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span) pairs, absorbing entire previously-resolved spans whenever today's price qualifies.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The returned spans are 1,1,1,2,1,4,6, matching the expected sequence.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) amortized per call, O(n) total across n calls: each (price, span) pair is pushed exactly once and popped at most once.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case (a strictly decreasing price sequence, where nothing ever gets absorbed).

When today's price is >= a stack-top entry's price, EVERY day that entry's span already covers is, by transitivity, ALSO <= today's price (since today is even higher than that entry, which was itself >= everything in its own span). This means absorbing that entry's WHOLE span in one step is exactly as correct as re-checking each of those days individually, just far faster, since it skips directly past an entire already-resolved chunk of history.

items: Each stack entry stores BOTH the price AND its already-resolved span, which is exactly what makes wholesale absorption possible without re-walking individual days.
The while loop's condition (top price <= today's price) directly matches the span definition's "<=" comparison.
Pushing today's own (price, span) pair at the end makes it available for FUTURE calls to potentially absorb in the same manner.

blocks.text: When a "streaming"/"online" problem asks for something like "how far back does a monotonic run extend," storing PRECOMPUTED aggregate information (like a span) alongside each stack entry lets a new element absorb an entire prior resolved run in one step, rather than re-deriving it day by day.

items: Storing only the price on the stack (not the span), forcing a recomputation from scratch that loses the amortized efficiency entirely.
Using a strict > instead of >= in the absorption condition, which would incorrectly fail to extend the span when today's price exactly EQUALS a previous day's.
Forgetting to push today's own (price, span) pair after resolving it, breaking the ability for FUTURE days to absorb today's span.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["The very first call to next","Always returns span 1, since there are no prior days to compare against"],["A strictly increasing sequence of prices","Each new price absorbs everything before it, so spans grow: 1, 2, 3, 4, ..."],["A strictly decreasing sequence of prices","Every price gets span exactly 1, since nothing before it ever qualifies for absorption"]]}

items: Explicitly explaining the "absorb an entire prior resolved span in one step, via transitivity" insight is what distinguishes the optimal amortized O(1) solution from a naive O(n)-per-call implementation.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Streaming/online: for each NEW value, find how far back a monotonic run extends" points toward a monotonic stack that stores PRECOMPUTED aggregate spans, not just raw values.

items: Why is the amortized complexity O(1) per call, despite the while loop appearing unbounded? Because each (price, span) pair is pushed exactly ONCE across the entire sequence of calls, and can only ever be popped once, bounding the TOTAL work across all calls to O(n).

How would you adapt this if the span needed to be "strictly less than" instead of "less than or equal to"? Change the absorption condition from <= to <, so equal prices would no longer extend the span.

How does this problem's technique compare to Next Greater Element I? Both use a monotonic stack, but this problem additionally stores an AGGREGATE value (the span) alongside each entry, enabling wholesale absorption rather than a simple one-to-one match.

A monotonic stack pattern augmented with aggregate data per entry (the span), a technique that generalizes to other "streaming, monotonic-run" problems beyond the simpler one-to-one matching seen in Next Greater Element I.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) per call, O(n^2) total time; O(n) space.
Optimized (monotonic stack, absorb whole spans): O(1) amortized per call, O(n) total time; O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic decreasing stack storing aggregate (price, span) pairs
Core Idea: When today's price is >= a stack entry's price, that entry's ENTIRE previously-resolved span can be absorbed in one step (by transitivity), rather than re-walking individual days
Time: O(1) amortized per call
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Storing the span alongside each stack entry is what enables wholesale absorption of an entire prior run, instead of a naive day-by-day recount
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Monotonic stack of (price, span); while top price <= today, pop and ADD its span; push (today, accumulated span)
